sections.title: Ocean in Motion
sections.text: Ocean in Motion is open. Look for flamboyant cuttlefish in the display they share with fish and corals. Scan along the edges of the viewing window if guests are having trouble spotting them. The update reports ocellaris clownfish in the anemonefish display. The proposed saddleback anemonefish identification there and pink anemonefish identification in the main reef tank are tentative.

sections.title: White seabass in Monterey Bay Habitat
sections.text: Aquarium staff identified the striped fish in the main Monterey Bay Habitat exhibit as white seabass (Atractoscion nobilis). White seabass belong to the drum family (Sciaenidae). Young fish can show dark bars that fade in adults. White seabass eat small fish and squid. The update suggests that more squid might help explain recent local sightings. This is a proposed explanation.

sections.title: Species highlight · Ocellaris clownfish
sections.text: The ocellaris clownfish (Amphiprion ocellaris), or common clownfish, lives on shallow reefs in the Indo-West Pacific. The update lists a maximum length of about 4.3 inches and a depth range of roughly 3–60 feet. It feeds on small planktonic animals and algae. In an anemonefish group, the largest fish is typically the breeding female and the next largest is the breeding male. When the female disappears, the breeding male can become female. The male tends the eggs near the host anemone, fanning them and removing compromised eggs. The update reports about 100–1,000 eggs and hatching in roughly 6–8 days, depending on temperature. The anemone shelters the fish among its stinging tentacles. The fish can provide nutrients through its waste. Research on the fish’s mucus, including low levels of particular sialic acids, offers clues to how the fish avoids triggering stinging cells. The role of microbes and acclimation remains an active research question. Guest prompt: Can you spot the largest clownfish near the anemone?

sections.title: Bay Watch · Nov 5–11
sections.text: The update reports migrating humpbacks, common dolphins, and juvenile makos breaking the surface. It also reports nighttime hydrophone detections of blue, sperm, and beaked whales. The list below records reported sightings for the week.
